concepts.name: Anekantavada: Core Doctrine of Many-Sidedness
key_dimensions: Literal meaning: 'Aneka' (many) + 'Anta' (aspects) + 'Vada' (doctrine) — distinction from monistic schools
Philosophical basis: rejection of absolutism (Ekantavada) in both Vedantic and Buddhist traditions
Anekantavada as a metaphysical claim vs. Syadvada as its logical/linguistic expression — UPSC trap: treating them as identical
Comparison with Buddhist Madhyamaka (Sunyavada) — both reject absolutism but differ in ontological commitments

concepts.name: Syadvada: The Doctrine of Conditional Predication
key_dimensions: Literal meaning: 'Syat' (perhaps/may be) as a qualifier — not skepticism but epistemic humility
Function: linguistic tool to express the multi-faceted nature of reality without contradiction
Distinction between Syadvada (theory of conditioned assertion) and Saptabhangi (its seven-fold application) — common UPSC confusion
Relationship to Anekantavada: Syadvada is the verbal/logical expression; Anekantavada is the metaphysical foundation

concepts.name: Saptabhangi Naya: The Seven-Fold Predication
key_dimensions: Seven modes: Syat-asti, Syat-nasti, Syat-asti-nasti, Syat-avaktavya, Syat-asti-avaktavya, Syat-nasti-avaktavya, Syat-asti-nasti-avaktavya
The role of 'Avaktavya' (inexpressible) — simultaneous assertion and negation that transcends linguistic limits
Logical structure: how Jains avoided contradiction using conditional qualification 'Syat'
UPSC trap: confusing Saptabhangi with Syadvada — Saptabhangi is the systematic application, not a separate doctrine

concepts.name: Nayavada: The Doctrine of Partial Standpoints
key_dimensions: Definition: a 'Naya' is a partial viewpoint (not false, but incomplete) — contrast with Pramana (valid knowledge)
Seven Nayas: Naigama, Sangraha, Vyavahara, Rijusutra, Shabda, Samabhirudha, Evambhuta — each captures one aspect of reality
Nayavada as epistemological tool vs. Anekantavada as metaphysical stance — hierarchical relationship
UPSC angle: Nayavada's relevance to pluralism and tolerance in Indian philosophical tradition

concepts.name: Pramana in Jain Epistemology: Sources of Valid Knowledge
key_dimensions: Two-fold Pramana: Pratyaksha (direct) and Paroksha (indirect) — differs from Nyaya's four-fold classification
Jain Pratyaksha includes Avadhi, Manahparyaya, and Kevala Jnana — supernatural perception accepted unlike in Nyaya-Vaisheshika
Paroksha includes Smriti, Pratyabhijna, Tarka, Anumana, Agama — comparison with other schools
UPSC trap: Jain direct perception (Pratyaksha) is broader than Nyaya's — includes extrasensory knowledge

concepts.name: Kevala Jnana: Omniscience as the Highest Knowledge
key_dimensions: Definition: perfect, infinite, direct knowledge of all substances and their modes simultaneously
Attained only by liberated souls (Siddhas) and Tirthankaras — epistemological and soteriological significance
Contrast with limited human knowledge — justification for Anekantavada (no finite being can claim absolute truth)
Relation to the Jain theory of soul (Jiva) — knowledge as intrinsic quality of soul, obscured by Karma

concepts.name: Jain Theory of Reality (Sat): Substance and Its Modes
key_dimensions: Reality defined as 'Utpada-Vyaya-Dhrauvya' — simultaneous origination, destruction, and permanence
This triadic nature of existence underpins Anekantavada — reality cannot be captured by a single predicate
Contrast with Buddhist momentariness (only change) and Vedantic permanence (only being)
UPSC angle: how Jain ontology avoids both eternalism (Sassatavada) and annihilationism (Ucchedavada)

concepts.name: Anekantavada vs. Buddhist Sunyavada: Key Distinctions
key_dimensions: Sunyavada: all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (Svabhava-shunya); Anekantavada: reality has multiple real attributes
Nagarjuna's critique: any 'Syat' predication still implies a fixed referent — Jain response via Nayavada
Both reject absolute monism but Jainism affirms real plurality of substances unlike Madhyamaka
UPSC trap: both are non-absolutist but Jainism is realist; Buddhism (Madhyamaka) tends toward anti-realism

concepts.name: Anekantavada vs. Advaita Vedanta: Absolutism Debate
key_dimensions: Advaita posits one absolute reality (Brahman); Anekantavada rejects any single-attribute absolute
Shankara's critique of Jain logic: Syadvada leads to self-contradiction if applied to itself
Jain counter: 'Syat' is a qualifier, not an absolute negation — avoids the self-refutation charge
UPSC angle: this debate illustrates the broader Indian philosophical tension between monism and pluralism

concepts.name: Anekantavada as a Theory of Tolerance and Pluralism
key_dimensions: Philosophical basis for Jain religious tolerance — no single doctrine can claim absolute truth
Influence on Indian composite culture: Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi, Gandhi's Sarva Dharma Samabhava
Gandhi's debt to Anekantavada — explicitly acknowledged; shaped his concept of truth (Satya) as multi-dimensional
UPSC angle: contemporary relevance to inter-religious dialogue, constitutional secularism, and pluralism

concepts.name: Syadvada and the Problem of Self-Refutation
key_dimensions: Classical objection: if all knowledge is conditional, is Syadvada itself only conditionally true? — Vicious regress
Jain response: Syadvada applies to empirical knowledge; Kevala Jnana of Tirthankaras is unconditional
Distinction between first-order claims (about world) and meta-level epistemological claims
UPSC trap: this objection is often attributed to both Vedantins and Buddhist logicians — know the sources

concepts.name: Karma Theory and Its Epistemological Implications in Jainism
key_dimensions: Karma in Jainism is physical (Karma-pudgala) — unique among Indian schools; obscures soul's inherent knowledge
Jnana-avaraniya Karma: specifically obscures knowledge — epistemological karma categories
Connection to Anekantavada: finite knowledge is karma-conditioned; only Kevala Jnana is karma-free and absolute
UPSC distinction: Jain karma is material/physical vs. Hindu karma which is action/consequence-based

concepts.name: Jain Categories of Knowledge (Jnana): Five-Fold Classification
key_dimensions: Five types: Mati (sensory + mind), Shruta (scriptural/testimony), Avadhi (clairvoyance), Manahparyaya (telepathy), Kevala (omniscience)
First two are Paroksha (indirect); last three are Pratyaksha (direct) — counter-intuitive for UPSC aspirants
Mati and Shruta can be valid (Pramana) or distorted (Naya) depending on conditionality
UPSC trap: Shruta Jnana in Jainism includes inference and testimony — broader than common usage of 'scriptural knowledge'

concepts.name: Philosophical Significance of 'Syat' as a Logical Qualifier
key_dimensions: 'Syat' means 'in some respect' or 'from a certain standpoint' — not probabilistic 'maybe'
Prevents Durnaya (absolutist fallacy) — the error of treating a partial view as the whole truth
Comparison with Western perspectivism (Nietzsche) and Wittgenstein's language games — useful for essay questions
UPSC angle: 'Syat' as a methodological safeguard against dogmatism in both philosophy and governance

concepts.name: Anekantavada and Gandhian Philosophy: Direct Lineage
key_dimensions: Gandhi's Jain mentor Shrimad Rajchandra introduced him to Anekantavada — biographical angle
Gandhi's concept: 'My truth is not THE truth' — direct application of Syadvada to political dialogue
Influence on satyagraha: willingness to hold firm to one's truth while respecting opponent's perspective
UPSC angle: questions linking Indian philosophical schools to modern political thought and national movement

concepts.name: Jain Epistemology vs. Nyaya-Vaisheshika Epistemology: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Nyaya accepts four Pramanas (Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, Shabda); Jainism uses two broad categories
Nyaya's realism is atomistic and categorical; Jain realism is holistic and modal (Paryaya vs. Dravya)
Both are realist schools but Nyaya accepts God (Ishvara) as a Pramana source; Jainism rejects theistic epistemology
UPSC trap: both are classified as 'realist' schools — key distinguishing features must be memorized precisely

concepts.name: Dravya, Guna, and Paryaya: Ontological Framework Supporting Anekantavada
key_dimensions: Dravya (substance), Guna (quality), Paryaya (mode) — every substance has permanent qualities and changing modes
This framework explains why both 'is' and 'is not' can be predicated of the same object in different respects
Six Dravyas: Jiva, Pudgala, Dharma, Adharma, Akasha, Kala — Jainism's unique ontological pluralism
UPSC angle: Jain ontology as foundation for Anekantavada — shows epistemology and metaphysics are inseparable

concepts.name: Syadvada's Influence on Indian Logic and Dialectics
key_dimensions: Jain logicians like Siddhasena Divakara, Samantabhadra, Haribhadra Suri developed formal Syadvada logic
Contribution to Indian Pramana-shastra (theory of valid knowledge) — often overlooked in favor of Nyaya
Hemachandra's synthesis of Anekantavada with grammar and poetics — interdisciplinary application
UPSC angle: Jain contribution to Indian intellectual tradition beyond religion — logic, mathematics, linguistics

concepts.name: Anekantavada: Distinction from Relativism and Skepticism
key_dimensions: Relativism: all views are equally valid; Anekantavada: all views are partially valid — crucial difference
Skepticism: no knowledge is possible; Anekantavada: comprehensive knowledge is possible (via Kevala Jnana)
Jains use Anekantavada to synthesize opposing views, not to dissolve truth claims entirely
UPSC trap: MCQs may describe Anekantavada as 'relativism' — this is incorrect; it is epistemic pluralism, not relativism

concepts.name: Textual Sources of Jain Epistemology: Agamas and Philosophical Treatises
key_dimensions: Canonical basis: Agamas (12 Angas) — Acharanga Sutra, Sutrakritanga contain epistemological discussions
Key philosophical texts: Tattvartha Sutra (Umasvati) — first systematic Jain philosophy text accepted by both Digambaras and Shvetambaras
Pramana-naya-tattvalokalankara (Akalanka), Nyayavatara (Siddhasena) — advanced logical treatises
UPSC angle: Tattvartha Sutra's unique cross-sectarian acceptance makes it the most important single Jain philosophical text
